events.text: Under the nine storeys you find something new in yourself: not only holding the five phases, but turning them. The strong one can feed the next. Wood can give itself to fire, fire to earth, earth to metal, metal to water, water to wood. You feel the wheel under your heart like a millstone, waiting to be pushed.

choices.text: Push it, once, gently

effects.log: Earth feeds metal. Your own strength goes round the wheel and comes out as a good year for the smithies and the mines, and a clean bright autumn. It works. You have turned the world a tenth of an inch. (Earth -2, Metal +2)

choices.text: Study it first

effects.log: A whole year of watching the five flow into each other, the way a miller watches the water before touching the wheel. When you do turn it, you will know exactly how far.

events.text: You have been turning the wheel for years now, and you notice something you did not expect: every turn costs the strong phase, and the strong phase is somebody's. The forges you cool are a smith's living. The spring you hold back is a farmer's orchard.

choices.text: Turn it anyway; the whole matters more

effects.log: Wood feeds fire. An orchard has a thin year so a cold valley can have a warm one. The orchard keeper curses the weather. You carry the curse. (Wood -2, Fire +2, Weight +2)

choices.text: Turn it more slowly, a little at a time

effects.log: A finger a year, not a hand. Nobody's living is broken. The wheel takes longer to even out. A centre that turns the world must turn it slowly enough for people to keep their feet. (Water -1, Wood +1)

events.text: For one season, by luck and work, the wheel is even: all five phases nearly level, nothing overrunning anything. The world is very quiet. Spring hands to summer, summer to the long days, the long days to autumn, autumn to winter, without a quarrel.

choices.text: Hold still and feel it

effects.log: It is like being a struck bell that has finished ringing: perfectly still, perfectly full. It will not last. You hold it as long as it does.

choices.text: Remember exactly how it feels

effects.log: You fix it at your middle: this is what even feels like. You will need to find your way back to it, again and again, for the rest of your life.

events.text: You have left the house, and the throne-hall ceiling knows it first. The painted dragons over the throne are only paint now. The old ministers look up at them during audiences, and look at each other, and say nothing.

choices.text: Let them see it is only paint

effects.log: Gold leaf and mineral blue and a little glue. The court looks up and sees it plainly for the first time. It is a strange kind of honesty, for a ceiling.

choices.text: Leave a little warmth up there anyway

effects.log: Not for the house. For the painters, long dead, who put you there. The gold stays faintly warm. The ministers still look at each other.

events.text: The ruler of the house has noticed. Every night now the ruler comes into the empty throne hall and stands under the ceiling and asks it to come back. Not in the crypt: here, looking up, at the paint.

choices.text: Answer from the floor, not the ceiling

effects.log: "I was never up there," you say, from under the throne. The ruler starts, and looks down, and does not understand. A house that looks for its dragon in paintings has forgotten where the ground is.

choices.text: Stay silent; you have chosen

effects.log: Silence, every night. The ruler stops coming after a year. The house goes on running down. You chose, and you are keeping the choice. (Weight -2)

events.text: A new reign, a new hall, and a new painter on the scaffolding with gold leaf, painting a dragon on the ceiling over a throne you do not hold. The painter has never seen you and paints you anyway, from the old patterns.

choices.text: Go up into the new paint

effects.log: You go up, and the gold is warm again, and the new house feels it on the backs of their necks. You chose to come back. It is heavy. It is right, perhaps. (Weight +2)

choices.text: Let the new dragon be only a painting

effects.log: A beautiful painting of a dragon. It is enough for the new house. They never know the difference. You are learning that a house can stand on a picture of you. (Weight -2)

events.text: A king you upheld is dead, and before dawn heaven sends you down to the hill east of the capital. The king is there in court robes, waiting on the grass, not afraid. Below, the city is waking, and the first people are coming out onto the roofs and looking east.
events.arc: The Hill East of the Capital

choices.text: Lower your head to the hill, and carry the king up

effects.log: The king steps onto your head as onto a stair, and you rise. The whole city sees it at once and a great shout goes up off the roofs. At the edge of heaven the king steps off and bows, and you come back down to the centre, lighter. (Weight -10)

choices.text: Talk with the king on the hill first

effects.log: You sit on the hill together, the dead king and the dragon, while the sun comes up. The king tells you what it was like, being stood on you. You tell the king what it was like, being stood on. Then the light reaches the roofs, and it is time. You lower your head to the hill, the king steps up as onto a stair, and you rise. At the edge of heaven the king steps off and bows, and you come back down to the centre, lighter. (Weight -10)

events.text: The people of the capital have started to climb the eastern hill at dawn on the anniversary of the king's death, to look at the sky. A shrine is going up at the top: one stone, flat, the shape of a dragon's head, where the king is said to have stepped.
events.arc: The Hill East of the Capital

choices.text: Keep the stone warm at dawn

effects.log: Every anniversary at dawn the stone is warm, and the climbers put their hands on it, and are glad. It is a very small thing to keep. It is one of the best.

choices.text: Let the hill be only a hill

effects.log: The stone is cold, and the climbers come anyway, and remember a good king. Memory does not need you to be warm. (Weight -2)

events.text: You have carried a king up now, and you understand something about the house you could not before: a house is not the palace or the throne or the seal. It is a line of people who were stood on you, one after another, and then set down. You held each of them. You set each of them down.
events.arc: The Hill East of the Capital

choices.text: Set the next one down gently, too

effects.log: Whoever comes next, you will carry them, and then you will let them go at the edge of heaven, and come back. That is the work. You are good at the first half. You are learning the second.

choices.text: Wonder whether you could go up with one, and stay

effects.log: At the edge of heaven, with a good king on your head, you could keep going. Nobody would stop you. The centre would be empty, and someone else would come. You put the thought at your middle. It is a dangerous thought. It is a beautiful one.

events.text: The new abbot of the Temple of the Yellow Dragon is {npc}, a farmer's child who came to the temple at nine to escape a famine and never left. {npc} has heard the old abbots' stories and does not quite believe them, and comes to the centre stone at midnight to test the floor with a plain question: are you hungry?
events.arc: The Abbot of the Nine Storeys

choices.text: "No. But thank you for asking"

mem.note: said thank you through the centre stone

effects.log: {npc} sits down on the stone very suddenly. Then laughs, the laugh of a farmer's child who has been proved right about something absurd. Nobody has ever asked you that before. It is the kindest question in all your years.

choices.text: "Sometimes. For rain, mostly"

effects.log: {npc} nods as if this were the most natural answer in the world, and that summer has the monks carry a bucket of well water to the centre stone every morning and pour it into the socket. You do not need it. You enjoy it enormously.

events.text: {npc} has a harder question tonight. The court wants the temple to pray for victory in a war of conquest. The monks are divided. {npc} sits on the centre stone and asks: is the pagoda a prayer for peace, or a threat to the nine nations? What were you built for?
events.arc: The Abbot of the Nine Storeys

choices.text: "For peace. Whatever they told the envoys"

effects.log: {npc} goes to the palace the next day and refuses the victory prayers, politely, and offers prayers for a short war and a fair peace instead. The court is furious. The abbot is not dismissed. Some of the generals are relieved.

choices.text: "I was built for whatever they needed. Decide what they need now"

effects.log: {npc} sits up all night. In the morning the abbot calls the monks together and they decide, all of them, by argument. It takes a week. It is the temple's answer, not yours. (Weight -2)

events.text: {npc} is dying in the abbot's quarters and has asked to be carried out to the centre stone. The monks lay the old abbot on it in the moonlight. 'Well,' {npc} says to the stone, "I never did find out what you eat."
events.arc: The Abbot of the Nine Storeys

choices.text: "Rain, and rice, and kindness. You fed me well"

effects.npcPass: old age, on the centre stone of the pagoda
effects.log: {npc} laughs once, very softly, and closes both eyes on the warm stone, and the monks chant until dawn. The stone is warm all night under them.

choices.text: Be warm, without words

effects.npcPass: old age, on the centre stone of the pagoda
effects.log: Warm, all through, like a hearthstone. {npc} sighs, the way the cold sigh in front of a fire, and is gone by dawn.

events.text: The temple is casting a great bell: bronze from a hundred villages, pots and spoons and hairpins melted together, a casting pit dug in the yard over you, and a founder who has made three bells and broken two. It will weigh as much as forty oxen. It is going to hang over you for as long as it hangs.

choices.text: Hold the casting pit perfectly still

effects.log: The bronze goes in, glowing, and the ground does not move a hair for the three days it takes to cool. They break the mould and the bell is whole, and when they strike it the first time you feel the sound go through you from top to bottom, all of you, like a shiver of joy. (Metal +2)

choices.text: Warm the pit so it cools slowly

effects.log: Slowly, slowly, a week. The founder has never had a casting cool so evenly. The bell has a deep, warm voice that carries across three counties. (Fire +1)

events.text: The great bell rings at dawn and dusk, every day. You have come to feel it the way a body feels its heartbeat: not noticed, and missed the moment it stops. In a storm the monks ring it all night, for the fishermen on the coast.

choices.text: Ring with it, under the ground

effects.log: The bell rings and the ground answers, very low, so that the fishermen far out in the storm feel it through the hull before they hear it. Some of them steer by it. The monks never know why the bell carries so far.

choices.text: Listen to what the bell is made of

effects.log: Pots, spoons, hairpins, a dead child's silver bracelet, a soldier's buckle. A hundred villages, ringing. You know the voice of every one of them in the sound. You decide that wherever this bell goes, you will want to go with it.

events.text: An envoy of the horse peoples of the steppe, visiting the temple, stands under the great bell for a long time, and measures it with a rope, and asks the monks how much it weighs, and whether it could be moved. The monks laugh. You do not.

choices.text: Remember the envoy's face

effects.log: A face that measures a bell the way a farmer measures an ox. You fix it at your middle. Somewhere north, some day, horsemen will remember how heavy the bell was. So will you.

choices.text: Make the bell seem to weigh twice as much

effects.log: The rope the envoy throws over the beam sags as if a mountain hung on it. The envoy goes home and reports that the bell cannot be moved. It is not quite true. It buys the bell a few hundred years.

events.text: {npc} and the heir have quarrelled again, loudly, in front of the court: about a war, or a minister, or a tax, or the way the heir looks at the throne. You feel it through the palace floor, two weights pulling against each other on your back.

choices.text: Warm the floor between them until they sit down

effects.log: The pavilion floor is warm and the afternoon is long and both of them, without meaning to, sit down. Sitting people quarrel less. By evening they are only sulking.

choices.text: Stay out of it: a centre does not take sides in a house

effects.log: You lie still. They shout themselves hoarse and go to opposite ends of the palace. It is theirs to mend. They usually do, in their own time. (Weight -1)

choices.text: Shake the pavilion so they both remember the ground

effects.log: The pavilion lurches. Ruler and heir grab the same pillar. For a moment they are just two frightened people holding on to the same thing. It does not end the quarrel. It reminds them what they share. (Weight +2)

events.text: A courtier has seen you again, in the clouds over the royal hunt, or in a fish's scales, or in a cracked tortoise shell, and has painted it, and is presenting it to the throne as an omen of heaven's favour. The ruler is pleased. You were nowhere near any of it.

choices.text: Let the painting fade on the scroll by evening

effects.log: By dusk the painted dragon on the scroll is a pale smear. The court decides it was an omen of something else. The courtier is very quiet for a month.

choices.text: Let it pass; flattery is cheap

effects.log: Another false sighting in the annals. They pile up on you like dust on a beam: light, each one. Not light, all together. (Weight +1)

choices.text: Send the ruler a dream of the real centre

effects.log: The ruler dreams of a plain warm floor, no clouds, no scales, no omens. In the morning the ruler looks at the courtier's painting for a long time and says, mildly, "It does not look like that." The courtier does not understand.

events.text: In a life that was not yours, centuries from now or centuries ago, somebody stood over the centre stone of a ruined temple at night and stopped a band of diggers from taking the box. You feel the shape of that night in your own centre stone, as if someone had stood guard over it before it was laid.

choices.text: Stand guard in return

effects.log: Somebody guarded your heart in a time you will never see. You guard it now, for both of you. No thief ever gets as far as the chamber again while you lie here.

choices.text: Wonder who it was

effects.log: A martial artist, you think, with good hands and a stubborn back. Somebody who did not need to and did. You will never meet them. You think of them every time the stone goes cold at night.

events.text: In a life that was not yours, somebody took the relic box from under this stone, and it grew heavier at every step, and in the end they carried it back. You know the weight they felt. It is your weight. You put it in the box yourself, or you will.

choices.text: Forgive the thief before the theft

effects.log: They carried it back. That is the only part that counts. You keep the box a little lighter for anyone who ever means to bring it home.

choices.text: Keep the box heavy, as it was for them

effects.log: Heavy, then. It taught someone something once. It can teach again.

events.text: In a life that was not yours, somebody put the centre stone of this pagoda back in its place and sat on it until dawn, and by dawn they knew the stone was breathing. You are breathing now, under the stone, slowly. You have always breathed like this. Somebody noticed first.

choices.text: Breathe a little slower, for whoever sat there

effects.log: In, a season. Out, a season. Somebody, somewhere in time, is sitting on you in the dark and feeling it, and is not afraid.

choices.text: Keep the stone warm for the next one to sit

effects.log: The centre stone is always warm, in every season, and pilgrims sit on it without being told to. They do not know why. One of them, one day, will know.

events.text: The morning of the raising. There is no omen and no dark sky: only the great centre pillar, one tree, lying on its rollers by the socket, and two hundred craftsmen at the ropes, and {npc} at the head of them, checking every knot twice. It is a great weight. It will not rise by being looked at.

choices.text: Lend the ropes a little of yourself

effects.log: The ropes take the strain and the tree comes up, slowly, as if the ground itself were pushing from beneath. Two hundred people raised it. They will tell their grandchildren that it went up as though it wanted to.

choices.text: Hold the socket still, and nothing more

effects.log: The centre stone does not move a hair as the foot of the pillar comes down into it. It takes until dusk. {npc} sets the last wedge with a mallet, and stands back, and does not say a word. It is theirs.
